outputs.L1:
An X-ray imaging apparatus performs fluoroscopy by irradiating a subject M with X-rays at each location within a long-length imaging range, at a dose weaker than that used for long-length imaging, while moving an X-ray tube in a body-axis direction relative to the subject M before long-length imaging is performed. The long-length imaging is implemented by moving the X-ray tube 2 in the body-axis direction relative to the subject M.

At a location having a greater body thickness, the transmitted dose D1 is lower, and therefore the tube voltage is set to a high tube voltage V1. Conversely, at a location having a smaller body thickness, the transmitted dose D2 is higher, and therefore the tube voltage is set to a low tube voltage V2. The tube voltage for long-length imaging is set based on the X-ray dose transmitted through the subject M during fluoroscopy, such that the doses of X-rays transmitted through the subject coincide with each other at each location. Accordingly, imaging conditions for long-length imaging can be appropriately set in regions where the height, or body thickness, of the subject varies.
outputs.L2:
Before performing long-length imaging by moving X-ray tube 2 along the body-axis direction relative to subject M, the X-ray imaging apparatus carries out fluoroscopy at each position within the long-length imaging range. During this fluoroscopy, the subject M is irradiated with X-rays at a lower dose than that used for the long-length imaging.

At a position where the subject has a greater body thickness, the transmitted dose D1 is lower, so the tube voltage is set to a higher value, tube voltage V1. Conversely, at a position where the subject has a smaller body thickness, the transmitted dose D2 is higher, so the tube voltage is set to a lower value, tube voltage V2.

Using the X-ray dose transmitted through the subject M during fluoroscopy, the apparatus sets the tube voltage for the long-length imaging so that the X-ray doses passing through the subject are made substantially equal at the respective positions. As a result, appropriate imaging conditions for long-length imaging can be established even in regions where the height, or body thickness, of the subject varies.
outputs.L3:
Before performing long-length imaging, the X-ray imaging apparatus carries out low-dose fluoroscopy while moving the X-ray tube along the body axis of the subject. This preliminary fluoroscopy is performed using an X-ray dose that is lower than the dose used during the actual long-length imaging, thereby reducing unnecessary radiation exposure while still obtaining information needed to determine suitable imaging conditions.

During this low-dose fluoroscopy, the apparatus evaluates differences in body thickness at various positions along the subject. Based on this information, the apparatus adjusts the tube voltage of the X-ray tube. A higher tube voltage is selected for thicker regions of the subject, where greater X-ray penetration is required, while a lower tube voltage is selected for thinner regions, where less penetration is sufficient.

The tube voltage is set so that the transmitted X-ray dose remains substantially consistent across different locations of the subject, despite variations in body thickness. By controlling the tube voltage in this manner, the apparatus can establish appropriate imaging conditions for long-length imaging over a wide area of the body. As a result, even when the imaging region includes portions with significantly different thicknesses, stable image quality can be achieved while avoiding excessive radiation exposure.
outputs.L4:
An X-ray imaging apparatus is configured to perform long-length imaging of a subject, such as imaging over an extended region along the body axis, while setting suitable imaging conditions for different anatomical locations. Before carrying out the main long-length imaging operation, the apparatus performs a preliminary low-dose fluoroscopic scan. During this fluoroscopy, the X-ray tube is moved relative to the subject in the body-axis direction, and fluoroscopic images or dose-related information are acquired at a plurality of positions along the imaging range.

From the information obtained during the low-dose fluoroscopic scan, the apparatus estimates the body thickness or X-ray attenuation characteristics at each location. Because the thickness of the subject may vary significantly from one region to another—for example, between the chest, abdomen, pelvis, and lower limbs—the X-ray conditions required to obtain an appropriate image also vary. If the same exposure conditions were used over the entire long-length imaging range, thinner regions could be overexposed while thicker regions could be underexposed, resulting in uneven image quality.

To address this, the apparatus determines location-specific imaging conditions for the subsequent long-length imaging. In particular, the tube voltage is adjusted according to the estimated body thickness at each position. A higher tube voltage is selected for thicker regions where X-rays are more strongly attenuated, while a lower tube voltage is selected for thinner regions where less penetration is required. The adjustment is performed so that the transmitted X-ray dose reaching the detector becomes substantially uniform, or otherwise falls within an appropriate target range, across the different locations of the subject.

Once these conditions have been determined, the apparatus carries out the long-length imaging operation using the optimized settings. As the X-ray tube and detector scan along the subject, the imaging conditions are changed in accordance with the previously obtained positional information. This makes it possible to acquire images in which exposure is better matched to the subject’s anatomical variation.

As a result, the apparatus can reduce unnecessary radiation exposure in thinner regions while maintaining sufficient X-ray penetration in thicker regions. The system therefore enables more appropriate long-length imaging conditions to be set automatically and helps produce images with more consistent brightness, contrast, and diagnostic quality across the entire imaging range.
outputs.L5:
**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in the English language, but it is also one of the most important. As a definite article, “the” helps us point to something specific. When we say “a book,” we could mean any book, but when we say “the book,” we mean a particular one that the listener or reader can identify.

This simple word gives clarity and structure to communication. It helps connect ideas, define meaning, and guide attention. “The sun,” “the world,” “the future,” and “the truth” all feel specific and meaningful because of this small article.

Although “the” is often overlooked, it appears constantly in English writing and speech. Its frequent use shows how essential it is for making language precise. Without “the,” many sentences would feel incomplete, unclear, or unnatural.

In this way, “the” proves that even the shortest words can have great importance.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a patent-style abstract describing an X-ray imaging apparatus that performs preliminary fluoroscopy while moving an X-ray tube along a patient’s body axis to determine tube voltage settings for long-length imaging based on transmitted X-ray dose and body thickness.
counterfactuals.output: An X-ray imaging apparatus includes an X-ray tube configured to irradiate a subject with X-rays, an X-ray detector configured to detect X-rays transmitted through the subject, a moving mechanism configured to move the X-ray tube and the X-ray detector relative to the subject along a body-axis direction, and a control unit. The control unit performs preliminary fluoroscopy while moving the X-ray tube along the body-axis direction, acquires transmitted X-ray dose information from the X-ray detector at a plurality of positions, and obtains body-thickness information corresponding to the plurality of positions. Based on the transmitted X-ray dose information and the body-thickness information, the control unit determines tube voltage settings for respective imaging regions in long-length imaging. The apparatus then performs long-length radiographic imaging using the determined tube voltage settings, thereby enabling appropriate exposure control over an extended imaging range having different subject thicknesses.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize the invention in technical patent language: an X-ray system uses low-dose fluoroscopy before long-length imaging, measures transmitted dose at each position of subject M, and adjusts tube voltage so transmitted doses match across regions of different body thickness.
counterfactuals.output: An X-ray imaging system is configured to acquire a long-length radiographic image of a subject by performing preliminary low-dose fluoroscopic exposure prior to long-length imaging. During the fluoroscopic exposure, transmitted X-ray dose information is measured at a plurality of imaging positions along the subject. Based on the measured transmitted dose at each position, the system determines variations in X-ray attenuation attributable to differences in subject thickness or composition. A controller then adjusts an X-ray tube voltage for respective positions so that the transmitted dose during subsequent long-length imaging is substantially equalized across multiple regions of the subject. Accordingly, the system reduces variations in image density and improves continuity and diagnostic quality of stitched or long-length X-ray images while limiting preliminary exposure dose.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a detailed description of an X-ray imaging apparatus where the tube moves relative to the subject during long-length imaging, and prior fluoroscopy with weaker X-rays is used to set higher voltage for thicker areas and lower voltage for thinner areas.
counterfactuals.output:
An X-ray imaging apparatus includes an X-ray generation unit, an X-ray detection unit, a subject support, a motion mechanism, and a control unit configured to perform long-length radiographic imaging while varying X-ray irradiation conditions according to the thickness of the subject.

The apparatus is configured for imaging an elongated region of a subject, such as the entire spine, lower limbs, or another long anatomical region that cannot be covered in a single exposure field. During long-length imaging, an X-ray tube is moved relative to the subject along a predetermined travel direction, for example in a head-to-foot direction. The movement may be performed by translating the X-ray tube itself, by moving a tube support arm, by moving the subject table, or by coordinated movement of the X-ray tube and detector. A detector, such as a flat panel detector, is positioned opposite the X-ray tube with the subject located between them, and the detector acquires a plurality of partial images or continuous image data as the X-ray tube travels. The acquired image data is then combined to produce a long-length radiographic image.

Before the main long-length exposure is performed, the apparatus carries out a preliminary fluoroscopic scan using X-rays having a lower dose or weaker output than those used for the final radiographic imaging. In this preliminary fluoroscopy mode, the X-ray tube is moved relative to the subject along substantially the same imaging path that will be used during the main long-length exposure. While the weak X-rays are emitted, the detector obtains fluoroscopic image data or transmission data at a plurality of positions along the subject.

Based on the fluoroscopic data, the control unit determines an attenuation distribution or thickness distribution of the subject along the long-length imaging direction. Portions of the subject that attenuate the X-rays more strongly are identified as thicker or denser regions, while portions that attenuate the X-rays less strongly are identified as thinner regions. For example, the pelvis, shoulders, abdomen, or upper torso may be recognized as relatively thick portions, whereas the neck, lower legs, arms, or peripheral portions may be recognized as relatively thin portions.

The control unit then sets X-ray exposure conditions for the subsequent main imaging operation according to the detected subject thickness. In particular, the tube voltage applied to the X-ray tube is set higher for thicker regions of the subject and lower for thinner regions of the subject. The apparatus may also adjust tube current, pulse width, exposure time, filtration, or other irradiation parameters, but the tube voltage is specifically controlled so that regions requiring greater penetration are exposed at a higher kilovoltage and regions requiring less penetration are exposed at a lower kilovoltage.

During the main long-length imaging operation, the X-ray tube moves relative to the subject while the control unit changes the tube voltage in accordance with the previously determined voltage profile. When the X-ray tube reaches a position corresponding to a thick portion of the subject, the control unit increases the tube voltage to improve penetration and prevent underexposure. When the X-ray tube reaches a position corresponding to a thin portion of the subject, the control unit decreases the tube voltage to avoid excessive dose and prevent overexposure. As a result, the detector receives image data with more uniform signal levels over the entire long imaging range.

The apparatus may store the relationship between tube position and selected tube voltage as an exposure control map. This map may be generated from the preliminary fluoroscopic scan and used to synchronize voltage switching with tube travel. Position sensors, encoders, or motor control signals may be used to determine the instantaneous position of the X-ray tube, and the control unit may output voltage control commands to a high-voltage generator in real time as the tube moves.

The X-ray detector may acquire images intermittently at multiple positions or continuously while the X-ray tube is moving. If multiple partial radiographic images are acquired, the control unit or an image processing unit may correct for geometric displacement, magnification differences, and overlap regions, and may stitch the images together to form a single composite long-length image. If continuous acquisition is used, the apparatus may reconstruct a long-length image from sequential detector readouts corresponding to the moving irradiation field.

By using the low-dose preliminary fluoroscopic scan to estimate subject thickness before the main exposure, the apparatus can automatically determine an appropriate tube voltage distribution for long-length imaging. This reduces the need for manual selection of exposure conditions and helps obtain an image with consistent density and contrast across both thick and thin anatomical regions. In addition, because the tube voltage is lowered where high penetration is unnecessary, the apparatus can reduce unnecessary radiation exposure to the subject while maintaining sufficient image quality in thicker areas.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a patent abstract for a radiographic long-length imaging method that scans a subject M with fluoroscopy before imaging and determines imaging conditions by varying tube voltage V1/V2 according to body thickness so the transmitted X-ray dose is uniform.
counterfactuals.output: A radiographic long-length imaging method includes performing a fluoroscopic scan of a subject prior to long-length radiographic imaging, acquiring fluoroscopic image information along an imaging range, and determining a body-thickness distribution of the subject from the acquired information. Imaging conditions for the subsequent long-length imaging are set based on the determined body thickness distribution. In particular, an X-ray tube voltage is varied between a first tube voltage V1 and a second tube voltage V2, or within a range including V1 and V2, in accordance with changes in body thickness along the imaging range, such that a transmitted X-ray dose reaching an image detector is substantially uniform. The subject is then radiographically imaged over the long length using the determined imaging conditions. Accordingly, density variation in the obtained long-length radiographic image is reduced while enabling appropriate exposure control for different body-thickness regions of the subject.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain, in the style of a Japanese patent translation, how an X-ray tube 2 is moved in the body axis direction and low-dose fluoroscopy is performed beforehand to appropriately set long-length imaging conditions for regions of differing subject height/body thickness.
counterfactuals.output:
In the long-length imaging apparatus, prior to main long-length radiography, the X-ray tube 2 is displaced in a body-axis direction of a subject, and low-dose fluoroscopy is preliminarily executed at a plurality of positions in said body-axis direction.

More specifically, the X-ray tube 2 is moved along the longitudinal direction of the subject, for example from an upper-side region toward a lower-side region or in the reverse direction, while maintaining an opposed relationship with the X-ray detector. At each movement position, fluoroscopic irradiation is performed with an X-ray dose lower than that used for main imaging. Fluoroscopic image data thereby obtained is used for recognizing a transmission state of X-rays in respective regions of the subject.

Since the subject thickness differs depending on a region, such as a chest region, an abdominal region, a pelvic region, or a lower-limb region, appropriate imaging conditions are not uniform over the entire long-length imaging range. Therefore, based on the low-dose fluoroscopic image data acquired beforehand, an imaging condition setting unit determines, for each region in the body-axis direction, imaging conditions such as tube voltage, tube current, irradiation time, pulse width, dose, and/or image processing conditions. In this manner, a region having a relatively large body thickness is set to a condition capable of securing a sufficient amount of transmitted X-rays, whereas a region having a relatively small body thickness is set to a condition in which unnecessary exposure is suppressed.

Accordingly, even when the imaging target includes regions different in subject height or body thickness, long-length imaging conditions can be appropriately set in advance. As a result, in subsequent long-length main imaging, it is possible to obtain a stitched long-length image having reduced density unevenness and stable image quality over the entire imaging range, while suppressing an increase in radiation dose to the subject.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
